summary: Looks at the security threats of the 6to4 IPv6 transition mechanism from RFC 3056. Because 6to4 routers accept IPv6-in-IPv4 traffic from any node, threats include denial of service and easier spoofing of IPv6 addresses. The memo discusses how to mitigate them.

plainLanguage.summary: 6to4 carries IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets between IPv6 networks. RFC 3964 explains how that design can enable spoofing, denial of service and service theft, and gives checks that reduce some risks.

subtitle: The security risks of 6to4 tunneling and the checks routers should perform.

tldr.problem: 6to4 routers and relays accept tunneled traffic from broad sets of IPv4 and IPv6 senders, making spoofing and denial-of-service attacks possible.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the forwarding paths, analyzes attacks against 6to4 and native networks, and specifies address and encapsulation checks for routers and relays.
tldr.outcome: The checks prevent some attacks, but the memo says spoofing by an untrusted relay remains the hardest problem. It describes 6to4 as an interim mechanism.

today: RFC 3964 is an Informational memo published in December 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC describes 6to4 as an interim mechanism.

sections.title: Why 6to4 Has Security Risks
sections.content:
6to4 is an interim method for connecting IPv6 networks across the IPv4 Internet. It places the tunnel's IPv4 address inside an IPv6 prefix and carries IPv6 packets using IPv4 protocol 41.

The design allows 6to4 routers to accept and decapsulate packets from other 6to4 routers and relays, while relays accept traffic from native IPv6 nodes. These broad acceptance rules make it possible to spoof IPv4 or IPv6 addresses and cause denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: 6to4 carries IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets. Because routers and relays accept traffic from many senders, attackers may send packets with false addresses.

sections.title: How 6to4 Traffic Is Forwarded
sections.content:
Two 6to4 sites send traffic directly to each other over IPv4. The destination's 6to4 prefix, 2002:V4ADDR::/48, supplies the IPv4 address used for the tunnel.

Traffic from a native IPv6 node to a 6to4 site goes through a relay that advertises reachability for 2002::/16. Traffic from a 6to4 site to a native IPv6 destination goes through a configured relay or one selected using the IPv4 anycast prefix 192.88.99.0/24. The relay used in each direction may differ, so a 6to4 router cannot simply restrict incoming traffic to one known relay.
sections.plainLanguage: Two 6to4 sites can exchange tunneled packets directly. A relay forwards traffic between 6to4 and native IPv6 networks, and the return path may use a different relay.

sections.title: Attacks Against the Networks
sections.content:
The memo identifies denial of service, reflected denial of service and service theft. It also describes traffic laundering, where an attacker sends traffic through third parties to make its source harder to trace. Attacks may use forged Neighbor Discovery messages, spoofed source addresses, reflected replies or local IPv4 broadcast addresses.

A relay that sends a reply to a spoofed source can help direct traffic at another node. The memo says each attack packet produces at most one reply, so this mechanism has no amplification factor. Attacks can still be difficult to trace, and a relay operator may appear to be the source of abuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers may use 6to4 to disrupt a node, direct replies toward a victim, or hide where traffic began. The memo says each packet causes at most one reply, but tracing the sender can still be difficult.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation Checks
sections.content:
Before encapsulating IPv6 in IPv4, a router must check that IPv6 addresses pass sanity checks and that a 6to4 source address embeds the same IPv4 address as the tunnel source. A packet that is neither to nor from a 6to4 address is dropped.

When decapsulating, both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses must pass sanity checks. The embedded IPv4 address in a 6to4 source or destination must match the corresponding tunnel address. IPv4 addresses must be global unicast, not private, loopback, multicast, reserved or broadcast. IPv6 checks reject such ranges as fe80::/10, fec0::/10 and ff00::/8. Optional ingress filtering may add checks against false source addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Before accepting a tunnel packet, the router checks that its embedded IPv4 address matches the actual tunnel address. It also rejects private, reserved, multicast, broadcast and other disallowed addresses.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Limits
sections.content:
Several automatic tunnel mechanisms use IPv4 protocol 41, and packet headers do not identify which mechanism produced a packet. Running multiple automatic tunneling mechanisms on one node therefore makes strict checks difficult. The memo suggests using no more than one such mechanism per node or assigning different mechanisms to different IPv4 addresses.

The memo considers a deployment where every dual-stack site or ISP runs its own relay instead of using third-party relays. This could move trust back to each site, but would require support from sites that do not use 6to4 and would reduce the ease of deployment. The memo identifies legitimate-relay verification as the hardest unresolved problem; correct address checks fix only some of the threats.
sections.plainLanguage: Different tunnel mechanisms can look alike because they use the same IPv4 protocol number. Even with correct address checks, routers cannot reliably determine whether every relay is legitimate.
